title: Chicago Immigration Court Orders Six Abused Minors Deported Despite Pending Legal Protections
excerpt: Federal lawmakers and children's rights advocates say the removal orders violate due process protections for unaccompanied minors who fled abuse and abandonment, marking a break from decades of legal practice.
body:
• Six unaccompanied minors aged 12 to 17 were ordered deported by a Chicago immigration judge on August 27, despite pending applications for Special Immigrant Juvenile Status
  • Legal advocates say the Department of Justice has changed longstanding practice since June 2026, no longer pausing removal proceedings for children with pending SIJS petitions
  • Senator Dick Durbin and Rep. Mike Quigley attended the hearing and called the proceedings a "mockery of the justice system," with attorneys planning appeals to the 7th Circuit

Six unaccompanied immigrant children, some as young as 12, were ordered deported from the United States by a Chicago immigration court judge on August 27, drawing condemnation from federal lawmakers, legal advocates, and children's rights organizations who say the proceedings violated due process protections guaranteed under federal law.

The children, aged 12 to 17, all had pending applications for Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS), a legal pathway created by Congress to protect minors who fled abuse, neglect, or abandonment in their home countries. Despite those pending applications, Judge Shawn Abraham — who appeared remotely while the children attended in person — issued removal orders after hearings that lasted only minutes for each child, according to attorneys present.

A Break From Longstanding Practice

"Today, the Chicago Immigration Court ordered six of our children removed from the United States without due process," said Laura Smith, executive director of the Children's Legal Center, at a press conference held at the National Immigrant Justice Center. "These children fled to the United States seeking safety and protection from the horrors that no children should have to endure."

https://x.com/BlockClubCHI/status/2093156640476348769

Smith said the government's approach represents a departure from decades of practice. Historically, children with pending SIJS applications have been shielded from removal orders, with proceedings paused until their immigration cases were adjudicated. Since June 2026, however, immigration courts have stopped routinely pausing removal proceedings for children with pending SIJS petitions, according to the National Immigrant Justice Center.

The federal government has also accelerated hearing schedules, forcing children to appear in court every two weeks instead of a few times a year. Many of the affected minors are held in federal custody by the Office of Refugee Resettlement, living in government facilities and long-term foster care homes.

"What I saw today — and I practiced criminal defense for 17 years right here in Cook County — was a mockery of the justice system."

— Rep. Mike Quigley

Lawmakers Sound the Alarm

Senator Dick Durbin and Representative Mike Quigley attended the morning hearing and spoke out at the press conference alongside legal service providers and child welfare advocates.

"These kids, some as young as 12 years old are now being deported from the United States," Durbin said. "It's happening right here in the city of Chicago in the Loop. This is not what America is all about."

In July, two children who had already received approved SIJS status were ordered removed — a move advocates say is unprecedented. Ten children designated as abandoned by Illinois state family courts appeared at the August 27 hearing, with six receiving removal orders.

DOJ Defends Backlog Reduction Push

A Department of Justice spokesperson defended the proceedings, saying in a written statement: "The Biden Administration allowed millions of unvetted aliens into our communities and intentionally turned a blind eye to hundreds of thousands of unaccompanied alien children in need of care. Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration."

The fast-tracking of children's cases is part of a broader DOJ strategy under its Executive Office for Immigration Review, which has been speeding up asylum cases, scheduling mass hearings, and issuing removal orders at an accelerated pace across the country.

Legal Challenges Ahead

Advocates plan to appeal the removal orders to the Board of Immigration Appeals. If unsuccessful, attorneys will file emergency appeals with the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to halt deportations, according to Smith.

Illinois has taken steps to protect unaccompanied minors. Governor J.B. Pritzker signed Ashley's Law (HB4890), which allows detained unaccompanied children in Illinois to petition state courts for abuse, neglect, or abandonment findings — the first step in applying for SIJS protection. Previously, children could only pursue this pathway after being released from federal custody.

The cases come amid a broader national crackdown on immigration, with ICE recording nearly 50,000 arrests in July alone. For advocates, the fast-tracked deportation of children with pending legal protections represents a line that should not be crossed.

"When we have had special immigrant juvenile status, it has meant termination of removal proceedings, and that the child gets to apply for residency," Smith said. "The reason it's been that way the entire time that it's existed is because that is the law."
image_caption: A Chicago immigration court has ordered six abused minors deported despite their pending applications for legal protections.
nri_angle: Unaccompanied immigrant minors, including children from Central American countries who have been abandoned or abused, face deportation from US immigration courts despite qualifying for federal protections — a policy shift that raises broader concerns about due process for all immigrant families.
